engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Tactics: The Skewer
chess.body: A skewer is a reverse pin. A valuable piece is attacked, it moves, and the piece behind it is captured. Skewers happen on open files and diagonals. Rooks and bishops execute skewers. Pattern: Rook checks king → king moves → rook captures queen. Spot this on every open file.

wisdom.title: The Compound Effect of Small Moments

These stack. In 15 years, she'll feel either deeply loved or quietly neglected. Both are built today.

book.author: Charlie Munger
book.chapter: Mental Models: Think in Multiple Frameworks
book.lesson: Charlie Munger's approach to decision-making: build a 'latticework of mental models' from multiple disciplines. The person who only knows accounting sees every problem through accounting. The person who knows psychology, economics, biology, physics, and history sees the problem in full. Munger's rule: you need 80-90 mental models to think well. The key ones: compound interest (mathematics), evolution (biology), supply and demand (economics), confirmation bias (psychology), systems thinking (engineering). His most important: 'I never allow myself to have an opinion I can't defend with the strongest arguments on the other side.'
book.key_quote: The person with one framework is fragile. The person with many frameworks is antifragile — they see what others miss.
book.action: Pick one field outside finance to study this month: psychology, history, or biology. Look for one principle that applies directly to your FP&A work.
crux: Build a latticework of mental models from many disciplines. One-model thinking distorts every problem.
To the man with a hammer, every problem looks like a nail. Most professionals are that man.
Invert, always invert. Ask how to fail, then avoid that.
Know your circle of competence and stay inside it. The edge is knowing where the edge ends.
Incentives explain most behaviour. Look at the incentive before assuming intent.
The psychology of misjudgement runs about 25 standard biases. Learn them as a checklist.
Opportunity cost is the correct filter for every decision.
Sit on your hands. Great opportunities are rare; act rarely and heavily.
Avoid the three big destroyers: alcohol, leverage, and envy. Envy is the stupidest.
Multiply models: compound interest, scale, backup systems, breakpoints, critical mass.
A great business at a fair price beats a fair business at a great price.
Read constantly. Neither Munger nor Buffett knows a wise person who doesn't read all the time.
Be reliable. Unreliability cancels every virtue you have.
Take a simple idea and take it seriously. That is the whole method.
learnings: Avoiding stupidity beats seeking brilliance, and it is far more achievable.
Inversion surfaces risks that forward thinking never reaches.
Most bad decisions come from one model applied where it doesn't fit.
Patience is a strategy, not a personality trait.
examples: Munger's Costco analysis combines scale economics, incentive design, and psychology at once — no single-discipline read explains it.
See's Candies: Berkshire paid up for brand pricing power in 1972 and it returned over $2bn on a $25m outlay.
Munger rebuilt from a divorce, no money, and the death of his 9-year-old son to become a billionaire. Reliability compounded.
adapt: Invert the Dubai plan: what guarantees no offer by mid-2026? Then remove those causes.
Circle of competence: Indian equities and FP&A. Polymarket stays paper-only until 200 trades say otherwise.
Check incentives before trusting any financial content, including your own.
Sit on your hands when the regime filter says no. Not trading is a position.

speaking.drill: Read three sentences aloud and drop your pitch on the final word of each. Record and check you are not rising at the end.

interview_tech.q: Explain covenant headroom and how you monitor it.
interview_tech.a: Covenants are contractual ratios — typically net debt to EBITDA, interest cover, and sometimes minimum net worth — tested quarterly. Headroom is the distance between your forecast ratio and the limit. Monitor it forward, not backward: run the covenant calculation inside the rolling forecast so you see a breach two quarters out while you can still act. Post-IFRS 16, check whether the definitions are frozen GAAP or current GAAP — lease liabilities entering net debt has breached covenants that had nothing to do with performance.

interview_tech.q: What controls matter most in a 60-store retail environment?
interview_tech.a: Rank by exposure. Cash and tender reconciliation daily at store level with independent review; goods receiving matched three-way to purchase order and invoice, because that is where margin leaks; inventory counts on a rolling cycle rather than one annual heroic count; markdown authorisation limits by role; and user access in the ERP reviewed quarterly, especially for leavers. Segregation of duties is hardest at small stores — compensate with detective controls and exception reporting rather than pretending it exists.

interview_soft.q: What is your biggest professional failure?
interview_soft.a: Pick a real one with a number, not a disguised strength. The structure: what you owned, what specifically you got wrong, what it cost, what you changed in your process, and evidence the change held. The disqualifying answers are 'I work too hard' and any failure where the fault lands on someone else. If you cannot name the cost in money or time, it was not a real failure and they will know.

interview_soft.q: Where do you see yourself in five years?
interview_soft.a: Answer the real question: are you a flight risk and do you understand the ladder. Be specific about the next rung rather than the summit — 'Financial Controller for a multi-market group, then Finance Director with commercial ownership, then CFO. What I need in between is treasury depth and a full M&A cycle, which is part of why this role interests me.' Naming what you lack reads as self-aware, not weak.

cfo_field.q: Know your break-even by store, not by chain.
cfo_field.a: A chain at group-level profitability can be carrying a quarter of its estate below contribution. Compute store contribution — gross profit less rent, staff and directly attributable fixed cost — and rank it. Then, before closing anything: is the lease committed, what does the store contribute to online fulfilment in its catchment, and what is the exit cost. A negative-contribution store with four years left on a non-cancellable lease is usually cheaper to run than to close.

cfo_field.q: VAT in the GCC is a cash-flow instrument, not just a compliance task.
cfo_field.a: Registration thresholds, filing frequency and the timing of input recovery all move working capital. A group filing quarterly rather than monthly holds recoverable input VAT longer than it needs to. Know the filing calendar in every jurisdiction the group trades in, and know which entity holds the recoverable balance — a refund stuck in the wrong entity is cash you own and cannot use.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early king safety: castle by move 8, avoid leaving the king on e1 after 6…Nf6; it prevented a forced ...Qb6‑​b2 attack.

lichess_summary.session_summary: AKK_010’s sole loss came from a sloppy Sicilian Defense where you ignored basic development and let Black seize the centre with ...d5, resulting in a forced exchange that left you down a pawn and without compensation. Your play shows a chronic inability to complete piece coordination before launching attacks—stop forcing premature pawn storms and solidify your position with simple moves like Nf3‑d2‑e4 before opening lines. For your next session, study the fundamentals of the London System (1.d4 2.Nf3 3.Bf4) to build a rock‑solid structure and practice the “two‑move” checkmate patterns to convert any material edge you finally manage to obtain.

lichess_puzzle.tip: A passed pawn is a criminal that must be stopped or escorted home.
